newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais reports first half profit.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais reports first half profit.

text.p: Troubled bank Credit Lyonnais reported a first-half net attributable profit of 67 million francs ($12.9 million) on Thursday, helped by a controversial injection of public money.
The earnings were nearly double the 36 million franc net attributable profit the bank posted in the period a year earlier.

The state-controlled bank, still digging out from the effects of an expansion spree that nearly made it bankrupt, was spared the humiliation of a return to the red by a 3.9 billion franc state emergency aid package announced last week.

The aid was aimed was at removing the burden of most of the costs imposed on Credit Lyonnais as part of a state bailout last year. Without it, the bank had been expected to post a loss of at least two billion francs.
The results were delayed for a week to give Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative government time to win approval from the European Commission for the emergency help.
The bank, which the government wants to privatise as soon as possible, said net banking income -- the banking equivalent of turnover -- fell to 21.5 billion francs from 22.1 billion.

But on a like-for-like basis, stripping out the effects of last year's rescue and non-recurring items, net banking income rose 3.9 percent. Net operating profit rose 20.1 percent to 4.2 billion francs.

The results included a 35 million franc payment to the state under a so-called "return to better fortune" clause in last year's bailout that stipulated it must pay a third of its profits into public coffers until 2014.

Net operating provisions fell to 2.3 billion francs from 2.5 billion. The bank also made a provision of 1.3 billion to cover its restructuring under which it plans to cut its workforce by 5,000 by the end of 1998.

All four of its areas of activity were in profit for the first time since 1993. But results worsened in France, where margins remained under pressure in a fiercely competitive banking climate. In Europe overall, the situation improved with operating income up 23 percent on a like-for-like basis.
The government has said the emergency aid would be followed by a full-blown state rescue -- the third in three years -- to ready the bank for sale.
Credit Lyonnais rocketed in size during the late 1980s, then came crashing down to earth in the early 1990s when property values collapsed and economic growth in Europe evaporated.
The bank eked out a 13 million franc profit for 1995 after racking up losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.
The government said last week it would wait until the half-year figures to decide how much more public money it would pump into the bank but the sum is expected to be at least 10 billion francs.
By conservative estimates, the ultimate bill to taxpayers for keeping the bank alive is expected to hit at least 100 billion francs with some analysts estimating it could run as high as 125 billion.

Analysts have warned that there are still huge uncertainties about the bank's future. The European Commission, which reluctantly cleared last year's 45 billion franc rescue plan for Credit Lyonnais, is expected to impose new conditions on the bank in exchange for approving the fresh state aid.
And no suitors have yet emerged for the bank's hand.
The bank, which was ordered to divest many of its assets in exchange for European Commission approval of the second bailout, could be forced to spin off even more. ($1=5.183 French Franc) REUTER
